elements.id-string-8: Quantum interference is studied in a three-band model of pseudospin-one fermions in the $\alpha-\mathcal{T}_3$ lattice.
elements.id-string-9: We derive a general formula for magnetoconductivity that predicts a rich crossover between weak localization (WL) and weak antilocalization (WAL) in various scenarios.
elements.id-string-10: Recovering the known results for graphene ($\alpha=0$), we remarkably discover that WAL is notably enhanced when one deviates slightly from the graphene lattice, i.e. when $\alpha>0$, even though Berry's phase is no longer $\pi$.
elements.id-string-11: This is attributed to the presence of multiple Cooperon channels.
elements.id-string-12: Upon further increasing $\alpha$, a crossover to WL occurs that is maximal for the case of the Dice lattice ($\alpha=1$).
elements.id-string-13: Our work distinctly underscores the role of non-trivial band topology in the localization properties of electrons confined to the two-dimensional $\alpha-\mathcal{T}_3$ lattice.
elements.id-string-14: The interference of waves is so fundamental to physics that it unites various branches, including but not limited to optics, acoustics, quantum mechanics, solids, and cold atoms.
elements.id-string-15: In solids, if the disorder is sufficiently high, wave interference can lead to a complete suppression of electronic transport.
elements.id-string-16: This phenomenon is known as Anderson localization (AL)~\cite{anderson1958absence}.
elements.id-string-17: A precursor to AL, weak localization (WL) refers to the negative quantum correction to the Drude conductivity due to the interference of electron waves~\cite{altshuler1980magnetoresistance,bergmann1984weak}.
elements.id-string-18: In WL theory, the deviation to the conductivity is expanded in terms of the parameter $\lambda_F/l$ ($\lambda_F$ and $l$ being the Fermi wavelength and the mean free path, respectively).
elements.id-string-19: Since disorder is inevitable in nature, WL is the standard method to measure the phase coherence length as well as determine the relevant processes responsible for electron scattering~\cite{chakravarty1986weak,beenakker1991quantum}.
elements.id-string-20: Coupling the electrons to the magnetic field introduces a finite phase difference between the interfering waves, and hence, magnetoconductivity is a critical tool in the study of WL.
elements.id-string-21: In contrast to conventional WL, the presence of spin-orbit coupling can lead to phase shift via spin precession resulting in destructive interference of electron waves, thereby enhancing the conductivity.
elements.id-string-22: This phenomenon, termed weak antilocalization~\cite{hikami1980spin} (WAL), also occurs in Dirac and Weyl materials where pseudospin replaces the actual spin~\cite{suzuura2002crossover,khveshchenko2006electron,mccann2006weak,gorbachev2007weak,wu2007weak,gorbachev2007weak,tikhonenko2008weak,tikhonenko2008weak,tkachov2011weak,lu2011competition,lu2013intervalley,lu2014finite,fu2019quantum}.
elements.id-string-23: The Dirac and Weyl equations that originated in particle physics now describe the low-energy physics of materials such as graphene, Weyl semimetals, and Van der Waal structures, leading to their resurgence in condensed matter physics~\cite{neto2009electronic,sarma2011electronic,armitage2018weyl}.
elements.id-string-24: The band topology of these materials makes them of high interest, which leads to peculiar properties.
elements.id-string-25: For instance, the presence of $\pi$ Berry phase leads to the WAL effect in graphene~\cite{suzuura2002crossover,khveshchenko2006electron,mccann2006weak}.
elements.id-string-26: Recent experimental breakthroughs in Van der Waal heterostructures, such as the discovery of twisted bilayer graphene exhibiting flat bands, have further intensified research in this arena~\cite{cao2018unconventional}.
elements.id-string-27: Almost all the quantum interference studies in these materials so far have been typically based on a two-band model that mimics Dirac and Weyl physics.
elements.id-string-28: Specifically, it was pointed out in the two-band Dirac fermion that a crossover from weak antilocalization to weak localization occurs as the $\pi$ Berry phase reduces to zero with the inclusion of Dirac mass~\cite{lu2011competition}.
elements.id-string-29: The problem of quantum interference effects on localization properties in multi-band models is largely unexplored despite the prevalence of such systems in experiments.
elements.id-string-30: For instance, the $\alpha-\mathcal{T}_3$ lattice model~\cite{raoux2014dia} that synthesizes the Dirac and flat-band physics in a single model comprises a hexagonal lattice with atoms situated at the vertices of the hexagons and their centers, thus describing a three-band system of pseudospin-1 fermions (Fig.~\ref{fig:feyn-diag} (f).
elements.id-string-31: By varying the hopping parameter between two sublattices, one interpolates between graphene ($\alpha=0$) and the dice lattice ($\alpha=1$).
elements.id-string-32: The $\alpha-\mathcal{T}_3$ model can be realized in trilayers of cubic lattices, Hg$_{1-x}$Cd$_x$Te quantum wells and cold-atom systems~\cite{wang2011nearly, rizzi2006phase, malcolm2015magneto, serret2002vortex}.
elements.id-string-33: In this Letter, we solve the problem of quantum interference in pseudospin-1 fermions and examine the localization properties of electrons in the $\alpha-\mathcal{T}_3$ lattice, deriving a general formula for magnetoconductivity that predicts a rich crossover between localization and antilocalization in various scenarios.
